overview.text: Module objective: Learn how to identify, understand, prevent and fix security vulnerabilities in backend applications and REST APIs. Build the ability to protect user data, enforce permissions, prevent malicious requests, secure files, manage credentials and harden APIs before deployment.
A backend API is one of the most important security boundaries in an application.
Consider PrepSpaces as an example. A student logs into the platform and can access courses, lessons, enrollment information and learning progress.
A student changes a URL from /users/101/progress to /users/102/progress and sees another student's learning history.
An instructor modifies a request and changes their account role to ADMIN.
An attacker submits specially crafted input that manipulates a database query.
Someone uploads a malicious file disguised as a PDF.
A developer accidentally publishes a database password on GitHub.
An API allows any website to read sensitive responses through an incorrectly configured CORS policy.
These are not simply programming mistakes. They are security vulnerabilities that can expose user data, compromise accounts, damage databases or interrupt application services.
In this module, we will use a Java + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL course management API as our running example.
The objective is not just to learn what vulnerabilities mean. You will learn how they occur, how to recognize them, how to implement fixes and how to verify that the fixes actually work.

blocks.text: API security is the practice of protecting application programming interfaces against unauthorized access, data exposure, manipulation, abuse and disruption.
An API provides a communication channel between applications.
PrepSpaces Frontend | | HTTPS Request | v Backend API | +---- Authentication | +---- Authorization | +---- Input Validation | +---- Business Logic | v PostgreSQL Database
A backend API receives requests from clients, processes information and returns responses.
The problem is that an API cannot assume every incoming request is legitimate simply because it came from your frontend.
Call endpoints directly without using the frontend.
Use a script or another HTTP client instead of a browser.
Therefore, the backend must independently verify every important security requirement.
Imagine a student sends this request:
The application correctly authenticates the student.
However, the student changes the URL:
Suppose the API returns Student 102's private learning progress.
A valid login does not automatically give a user permission to access every resource.
API security must verify both identity and permissions.
A foundational security model is the CIA triad.
Confidentiality ensures that sensitive information is accessible only to authorized users.
Students cannot see other students' private profiles.
API responses do not reveal password hashes or internal secrets.
Private course materials are not accessible to unauthorized users.
Integrity ensures that data cannot be modified by people or processes without appropriate permission.
A student cannot change their account role to administrator.
A student cannot alter their course completion records.
An instructor cannot modify another instructor's course without permission.
An API cannot silently overwrite protected database properties.
Availability ensures that an API remains accessible to legitimate users.
Request size restrictions prevent unnecessarily large uploads.
Database connection pools are managed safely.
An API that stores private data securely but becomes unavailable because of uncontrolled requests still has a security problem.
These concepts work together but solve different problems.
Allow only authorized roles and resource owners

ADMIN ├── Manage users ├── Create courses ├── Update courses └── Delete courses INSTRUCTOR ├── Create permitted courses ├── Update own courses └── Manage own modules STUDENT ├── View permitted courses ├── Enroll in courses └── View own learning progress
These are example business rules. Your actual authorization policy must be explicitly defined.
A professional backend should follow these principles.
Give every user, service and database account only the permissions necessary for its tasks.
A student should not receive administrator permissions just because an endpoint accepts a user ID.
Do not assume access should be granted unless explicitly prohibited.
Instead, require a defined permission before allowing a protected operation.
For example, protect a course update operation using authentication, role checks, ownership checks, input validation and database constraints.
Never assume that a request is safe because it came from your own frontend.
Validate request bodies, query parameters, path variables, uploaded files and external API responses.
Use HTTPS to protect data transmitted between clients and backend systems.
Return only the data necessary for the requested operation.
Maintain useful records of suspicious activity without storing passwords, tokens or other sensitive values.
Key takeaway: API security is not a single authentication feature. It is a combination of controls protecting identity, resources, data, operations and infrastructure.
Threat modeling is a structured process for identifying possible security threats before attackers exploit them.
Instead of waiting for a vulnerability to appear, you examine the application from an attacker's perspective.
What information would an attacker want?
Which endpoints could expose that information?
Where does the application trust incoming data?
Which components communicate with each other?
What happens if an authorized user behaves maliciously?
What could happen if an external service is compromised?

Threat modeling should happen during system design and continue as the application evolves. OWASP provides a structured threat-modeling approach using system diagrams, threat identification and risk prioritization.
An attack surface is the collection of points through which an application can potentially be attacked.
Before identifying threats, understand how information moves through the application.
Email, payment, analytics and AI providers
The diagram helps identify where information crosses trust boundaries.
For example, incoming frontend data is untrusted. A response from a third-party API is also untrusted, even when it comes from a familiar provider.
STRIDE is a threat-classification technique commonly used to analyze application security.
It identifies six broad threat categories.
An administrator denies deleting a course
An attacker pretends to be a legitimate user.
A student's access token is stolen and used by another person.
An attacker modifies information without authorization.
A student modifies a request to change the course price or completion status.
A user denies having performed an operation.
An administrator deletes a course but later claims that they did not perform the operation.
Sensitive information becomes accessible to unauthorized users.
A course API accidentally includes private student email addresses in a public response.
An attacker overwhelms an application or its dependent resources.
An API allows unlimited generation of expensive AI reports or unlimited file uploads.
A user obtains permissions beyond their authorized role.
A student changes the request property:
If the backend accepts this property without authorization, the student may gain administrator privileges.
Identifying a threat is only the beginning. You must also prioritize it.
Use a scale from 1 to 5 for each factor.
BOLA affecting private student data should receive immediate attention.
This is a simplified prioritization model, not a formal security risk certification.
Every significant security concern should have a documented record.

When to use threat modeling: Before implementing a new authentication system, adding a file upload feature, designing an administrative API, integrating a payment provider or exposing new sensitive endpoints.
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project is a nonprofit foundation that provides application security education, standards and resources.
OWASP publishes security guidance for developers, security engineers and organizations.
One important resource is the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023 edition).
It identifies ten major API security risk categories.
3.2 The ten OWASP API security risks
API3: Broken Object Property Level Authorization
API6: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
Server fetches an unauthorized internal URL
Insufficient validation of external API responses
3.3 Understanding the risks beyond the individual lessons
Although this module teaches BOLA, BFLA, SQL injection and other selected topics separately, you should understand the full API security landscape.
An enrollment API might be technically secured but still abused through automated repeated requests.
You need business-level safeguards such as:
This occurs when the backend fetches a user-supplied URL without appropriate validation.
For example, a service that imports remote course images must not blindly fetch arbitrary URLs that could point to internal infrastructure.
An old endpoint must not remain publicly accessible simply because the frontend no longer uses it.
Responses from payment providers, AI providers and external systems must be validated before application logic trusts them.
A third-party response is data, not an instruction to bypass your security rules.

Key takeaway: The OWASP API Top 10 is a practical risk checklist. It helps you look beyond basic authentication and identify problems across authorization, infrastructure, business logic and external integrations.
BOLA stands for Broken Object Level Authorization.
It occurs when an API allows a user to access or modify an object without correctly verifying that the user has permission to perform the requested operation on that particular object.

BOLA is a major API security risk because APIs frequently retrieve database objects using identifiers provided by clients. OWASP identifies the need for object-level authorization checks in every function that accesses records using client-supplied identifiers.
The authenticated user is Student A.
@GetMapping("/students/{id}/progress") public Progress getProgress( @PathVariable Long id) { return progressRepository .findByStudentId(id); }
The controller accepts an ID from the client and directly retrieves the corresponding record.
It does not verify whether the authenticated user owns that record.
The user can modify the requested identifier and potentially access someone else's information.
The authenticated user's identity must determine which records they can access.
One approach is to provide a self-service endpoint:
@GetMapping("/me/progress") public Progress getMyProgress( @AuthenticationPrincipal AppUserPrincipal principal) { return progressService.getProgress( principal.getUserId() ); }
The identity comes from the authenticated security context, rather than from a student ID supplied by the client.
For resources identified by their own IDs, authorization must still check ownership.
Optional<Progress> findByIdAndStudentId( Long progressId, Long studentId );

public Progress getStudentProgress( Long progressId, Long currentStudentId) { return progressRepository .findByIdAndStudentId( progressId, currentStudentId ) .orElseThrow( ProgressNotFoundException::new ); }
Now the query retrieves a record only when both the requested resource ID and authenticated owner match.
This is stronger than simply trusting a student ID in the request.
Do not check ownership only on GET endpoints.
Creating a record against another user's account
Every operation that accesses a protected resource needs appropriate authorization.
Some developers believe changing IDs from integers to UUIDs makes unauthorized access impossible.
Random identifiers can make guessing harder, but they do not replace permission checks.
If someone obtains a valid UUID, the backend must still verify ownership.
OWASP explicitly warns that unpredictable identifiers alone are not sufficient to prevent BOLA.
Student A = ID 101 Student B = ID 102
Student A retrieves their own progress.
Student B retrieves their own progress.
Student A attempts to retrieve Student B's progress.
Student A attempts to update Student B's progress.
Student A attempts to delete Student B's progress.
Only operations authorized for the authenticated user should succeed.
Important: Test every relevant endpoint and HTTP method. Testing only one GET endpoint does not demonstrate that the entire application is protected.
BFLA stands for Broken Function Level Authorization.
It occurs when a user can execute an application function that they are not authorized to use.
BOLA is about accessing the wrong object.
BFLA is about accessing the wrong function.
Consider a platform with these endpoints:
A student should not automatically be allowed to perform administrative functions.
If the backend does not enforce these restrictions, a student might access privileged operations directly.
Fix: ownership and resource policy checks

@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/admin") public class AdminController { @PostMapping("/courses") public Course createCourse( @RequestBody CourseRequest request) { return courseService.create(request); } }
The controller has no authorization rule.
If the backend's global security configuration also allows this request, any authenticated user might be able to create a course.
The UI hiding the administrator button does not solve the problem.
An attacker can call the API directly.

@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/admin") public class AdminController { @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") @PostMapping("/courses") public Course createCourse( @RequestBody CourseRequest request) { return courseService.create(request); } @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") @DeleteMapping("/courses/{id}") public void deleteCourse( @PathVariable Long id) { courseService.deleteCourse(id); } }
Spring Security supports method-level authorization through annotations such as @PreAuthorize.
You should define permissions centrally rather than implementing inconsistent conditions in multiple controllers.

ADMIN ├── CREATE_COURSE ├── UPDATE_ANY_COURSE ├── DELETE_COURSE └── MANAGE_USERS INSTRUCTOR ├── CREATE_COURSE ├── UPDATE_OWN_COURSE └── MANAGE_OWN_MODULES STUDENT ├── VIEW_COURSE ├── ENROLL_COURSE └── VIEW_OWN_PROGRESS
Not all systems need the same roles. Some may use fine-grained permissions instead of fixed roles.
Test each protected operation with every relevant role.
You should also verify that a permitted instructor cannot modify another instructor's course. That becomes an object-level authorization check as well.
Key takeaway: Every privileged API function must enforce its permission on the backend. Never rely on frontend navigation, hidden buttons or URL obscurity.
SQL injection is a security vulnerability that occurs when untrusted input is incorporated into a database query in a way that changes the intended SQL structure.
Imagine PrepSpaces has a course search endpoint:
The backend uses the supplied title to construct a database query.
If the application combines raw user input with SQL strings, an attacker may be able to manipulate the query.
In certain configurations, further compromise of database-connected systems.

String title = request.getParameter("title"); String sql = "SELECT * FROM courses WHERE title = '" + title + "'"; Statement statement = connection.createStatement(); ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery(sql);
The SQL query structure is being created by combining a string with untrusted user input.
The database cannot reliably distinguish the developer's intended query from SQL syntax introduced through the input.
An attacker could supply specially crafted input intended to modify the query's meaning.
The root problem is not that the input contains unusual characters. The problem is that the application treats untrusted data as part of the SQL program.
6.3 Prevent SQL injection using prepared statements
The preferred solution is parameterized queries.
A parameterized query separates SQL instructions from user-provided values.
String sql = "SELECT * FROM courses WHERE title = ?"; PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(sql); statement.setString(1, title); ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery();
The SQL structure is defined by the application.
The title is passed as a parameter.
The database treats the supplied value as data rather than additional SQL syntax.
OWASP recommends parameterized queries as the primary defense against SQL injection.
6.4 SQL injection prevention with Spring Data JPA
For a Spring Boot application using Spring Data JPA, derived repository methods are useful.
public interface CourseRepository extends JpaRepository<Course, Long> { List<Course> findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase( String title ); }
The framework generates an appropriately parameterized query for the supplied value.
You can also use named parameters:
@Query(""" SELECT c FROM Course c WHERE c.title = :title """) List<Course> findCoursesByTitle( @Param("title") String title );
This separates the query structure from the supplied value.
Important: Using an ORM does not automatically prevent SQL injection if you manually construct dynamic SQL or concatenate user input into native queries.
There is a subtle problem with queries involving sorting.
SQL parameters generally represent data values, not table names, column names or keywords such as ASC and DESC.
Therefore, do not simply append arbitrary user-supplied values to an SQL statement.

private static final Set<String> ALLOWED_SORT_FIELDS = Set.of("title", "createdAt", "level"); public Sort createSort( String sortBy, String direction) { if (!ALLOWED_SORT_FIELDS.contains(sortBy)) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( "Invalid sort field" ); } Sort.Direction sortDirection; try { sortDirection = Sort.Direction.fromString(direction); } catch (IllegalArgumentException exception) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( "Invalid sort direction" ); } return Sort.by(sortDirection, sortBy); }
Here, the application controls which fields can be used.
OWASP specifically recommends allowlisting dynamic SQL structural elements that cannot be parameterized.
SQL injection is only one form of injection.
Passing raw input to shell commands
Untrusted input interpreted as template code
The same underlying lesson applies: data from untrusted sources must not unexpectedly become executable instructions.
Give database accounts only the permissions they require.
Validate input according to business requirements.
Do not reveal database error details to API clients.
Test database operations with hostile-looking but non-destructive input in an isolated environment.
Key takeaway: Parameterization is the primary protection against SQL injection. Input validation is additional protection, not a replacement for safe query construction.
Mass assignment occurs when an application automatically maps incoming request properties to internal objects without sufficiently restricting which properties the client is allowed to modify.
This can allow a user to change fields that should be controlled by the backend.
id name email passwordHash role accountEnabled createdAt
The frontend should allow a student to update:
But the backend accepts the entire entity from the request.
@PutMapping("/users/{id}") public User updateUser( @PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody User user) { user.setId(id); return userRepository.save(user); }
This directly binds incoming JSON to the database entity.
A malicious client may attempt to supply additional properties, including properties the user interface never exposes.
If these properties are accepted and persisted without authorization checks, the student may modify protected account information.
7.3 Why direct entity binding is dangerous
A database entity represents internal application state.
A request object represents the limited information a client is allowed to submit.
These are not the same thing.
A public API should not automatically expose all these properties for modification.
7.4 The secure solution: Data Transfer Objects
Use a DTO to define exactly which properties the client can send.
public record UpdateProfileRequest( @NotBlank String name, @Email String email ) {}

@PutMapping("/profile") public UserResponse updateProfile( @Valid @RequestBody UpdateProfileRequest request, @AuthenticationPrincipal AppUserPrincipal principal) { return userService.updateProfile( principal.getUserId(), request ); }

public UserResponse updateProfile( Long userId, UpdateProfileRequest request) { User user = userRepository.findById(userId) .orElseThrow(UserNotFoundException::new); user.setName(request.name()); user.setEmail(request.email()); User saved = userRepository.save(user); return new UserResponse( saved.getId(), saved.getName(), saved.getEmail() ); }
No role assignment from the request.
No direct modification of administrative status.
7.5 Mass assignment and excessive data exposure
There are two related security problems:
A user modifies a field they should not be allowed to change.
Example: Changing role from STUDENT to ADMIN.
A backend returns more information than the client needs.
The response exposes internal properties unnecessarily.
OWASP groups mass assignment and excessive data exposure within API3:2023, Broken Object Property Level Authorization.
Instead of returning database entities directly, construct explicit response objects.
public record UserResponse( Long id, String name, String email ) {}
The API now returns only the properties intended for that operation.
For an ordinary student profile update endpoint, test requests containing additional properties such as:
The response follows the documented API contract.
The application can either reject unexpected properties or ignore them, depending on its API policy. Regardless, protected properties must remain unchanged.
Key takeaway: Never let clients control the entire internal entity. Use explicit request and response DTOs, and assign protected properties through trusted backend logic.
CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing.
It is a browser security mechanism that controls whether a web page from one origin is permitted to read responses from another origin.
These are different origins because their hostnames are different.
The browser checks whether the API allows the frontend origin to access its response.
That decision is communicated through HTTP CORS headers.
Browsers apply the same-origin policy to restrict how scripts from one origin interact with resources from another origin.
CORS allows a server to explicitly permit certain cross-origin browser requests.
GET /api/courses HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Origin: https://frontend.example.com
HTTP/1.1 200 OK Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://frontend.example.com Content-Type: application/json
The browser sees that the requested origin is permitted and allows the frontend JavaScript to read the response.
For certain cross-origin requests, the browser first sends an OPTIONS request to check whether the intended method and headers are allowed.
OPTIONS /api/courses Origin: https://frontend.example.com Access-Control-Request-Method: POST Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://frontend.example.com Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Authorization, Content-Type
The browser can then proceed with the actual request, subject to the CORS policy.
Preflight handling is particularly important for requests using methods or headers that trigger the CORS preflight mechanism.
This permits any origin to read responses where that header is applicable.
It is acceptable for genuinely public, non-credentialed resources in appropriate circumstances, but it is usually unsuitable for private APIs.
An application might read the request's Origin header and automatically return it as an allowed origin without verifying it.
This is dangerous because arbitrary websites may then be permitted to read sensitive browser responses, especially when credentials are also permitted.
An API may enable credentialed cross-origin requests even though they are not required.
CORS is not an authentication or authorization mechanism.
A non-browser client can call an API without being constrained by browser CORS enforcement. Every API request must still be authenticated and authorized by the server.
CORS does not replace CSRF protection either.
8.6 Secure CORS configuration in Spring Boot

@Configuration public class CorsConfig { @Bean public CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() { CorsConfiguration config = new CorsConfiguration(); config.setAllowedOrigins( List.of("https://frontend.example.com") ); config.setAllowedMethods( List.of( "GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS" ) ); config.setAllowedHeaders( List.of( "Authorization", "Content-Type", "X-Request-Id" ) ); config.setAllowCredentials(false); config.setMaxAge(3600L); UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource(); source.registerCorsConfiguration( "/api/**", config ); return source; } }
Then integrate CORS with the Spring Security filter chain:

@Bean public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain( HttpSecurity http) throws Exception { http .cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth .anyRequest().authenticated() ); return http.build(); }
This example uses a bearer-token style request and does not require cross-origin browser cookies.
When cookie-based authentication requires cross-origin credentials, configure an exact trusted origin and enable credentials only where necessary. Also apply the appropriate CSRF protection.
Spring Security requires CORS processing to happen before its authentication checks for proper preflight handling.
Normal API security rules still apply
Allowed only under the configured policy
Also verify that a rejected browser origin does not lead you to assume that the actual server endpoint is protected from unauthorized direct requests.
Key takeaway: CORS controls browser-based cross-origin response access. It does not replace backend authentication, authorization or CSRF protection.

sections.title: 9. Secure File Upload and Download APIs

blocks.text: 9.1 Why are file APIs a security risk?
Many applications allow users to upload and download documents.
A course management platform might allow:
File handling creates security risks because the backend receives content that may not be trustworthy.
A file called assignment.pdf is not necessarily a genuine PDF.
Its filename, extension and declared content type can all be misleading.
Files designed to exploit vulnerable parsers.
Content that exposes users to unsafe downloads.
Suppose your API accepts any uploaded file:
@PostMapping("/upload") public String upload( @RequestParam MultipartFile file) { // Save file return "Uploaded successfully"; }
This does not prove that the uploaded file is actually a PDF.
The Content-Type value is supplied by the client and must not be treated as authoritative.
Using user-supplied filenames directly as storage paths can create path traversal vulnerabilities.
The application should generate its own storage identifiers.
An API that accepts unlimited file sizes can consume:
A secure file upload process should follow a defined workflow.
Authenticate the user and check upload permission
Size, permitted extension and actual file format
Malware scanning and content safety checks
Generate a server-controlled filename and store privately
Store owner, generated ID, format and scan status
A secure upload system should use multiple checks.
Inspect declared and detected file formats
Verify actual format using file content
Prevent unapproved files from being downloaded
For example, your course management platform might permit only:
The application should verify the actual file format as well as the extension.
Do not rely on the extension or Content-Type header alone.
OWASP's File Upload Cheat Sheet provides guidance on extension allowlists, file signatures, authorization, size limits and safe storage.
These are illustrative limits. Choose values appropriate to your application and enforce limits at the infrastructure or reverse-proxy layer as well.

@Service public class FileUploadService { private static final long MAX_SIZE = 10 * 1024 * 1024; private static final Set<String> ALLOWED_TYPES = Set.of( "application/pdf", "image/jpeg", "image/png" ); private final FileTypeInspector fileTypeInspector; private final MalwareScanner malwareScanner; private final PrivateFileStorage storage; public FileUploadService( FileTypeInspector fileTypeInspector, MalwareScanner malwareScanner, PrivateFileStorage storage) { this.fileTypeInspector = fileTypeInspector; this.malwareScanner = malwareScanner; this.storage = storage; } public String upload(MultipartFile file) throws IOException { if (file.isEmpty()) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( "File cannot be empty" ); } if (file.getSize() > MAX_SIZE) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( "File size exceeds the limit" ); } String detectedType = fileTypeInspector.detect( file.getInputStream() ); if (!ALLOWED_TYPES.contains(detectedType)) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( "Unsupported file format" ); } malwareScanner.scan(file); String storageKey = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); storage.store(storageKey, file); return storageKey; } }

This is an architecture example. FileTypeInspector, MalwareScanner and PrivateFileStorage must have real implementations. The scanner must fail closed when inspection cannot be completed, and uploaded content should remain quarantined until approved.
Notice that the application's storage identifier is generated independently from the original filename.
Do not automatically store uploaded documents inside a publicly accessible web directory.
Filesystem directories outside the web root.
Quarantine storage for files awaiting inspection.
For object storage, the public should not be able to retrieve private files merely by guessing their storage paths.
File downloads require their own authorization checks.
Does the user have permission to view it?
Is the file approved for download?
Is it associated with the correct course or student?
Is the download being delivered with safe response headers?
For sensitive files, return them as attachments where appropriate, set a controlled Content-Type, and use X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
A short-lived signed URL may be appropriate for private object storage, but remember that possession of that URL can grant access until it expires. Treat it as a temporary credential.
If ZIP files are supported, consider:
Avoid allowing HTML, SVG or other active content to be served from an origin with sensitive application cookies or privileges unless there is a carefully designed isolation strategy.
Verify that a user cannot overwrite another user's file by changing the identifier.
Key takeaway: Upload security means validating the file, controlling storage, scanning content and independently authorizing downloads.
Secrets are confidential values used by applications to authenticate themselves or access protected services.
A backend can have excellent authorization controls and still be compromised when an attacker obtains its secret credentials.
public class DatabaseConfig { private String username = "admin"; private String password = "myDatabasePassword"; }
This is dangerous because the credentials are embedded in application source code.
Imagine a developer commits the file to a public Git repository.
Anyone who obtains the source may also obtain the credentials.
Removing the password from the latest version does not necessarily remove it from previous Git commits.
Instead of hardcoding credentials, reference externally provided configuration.
At runtime, the application receives the relevant configuration through its deployment environment or secret-injection mechanism.
This separates application source code from sensitive configuration.
However, environment variables are not automatically a complete secrets-management solution. Their access, exposure, permissions and lifecycle must also be controlled.
A dedicated secrets-management system provides more control than manually distributing passwords.
Centralized secret storage, access policies, credential management and rotation.
Manages application secrets and supports credential rotation.
Stores and manages secrets for applications running on Google Cloud.
OWASP recommends centralized secret management, controlled provisioning, auditing, rotation and revocation.
A database connection does not necessarily need the database administrator account.

Backend Application | v Course API Database User | +---- Read permitted tables +---- Insert permitted records +---- Update permitted records | X---- Cannot manage database users X---- Cannot change database security configuration
Never reuse production credentials in local development or testing environments.
A secret should have a lifecycle.
Store it in an approved secret-management system.
Permit access only to authorized users and services.
Replace credentials according to their risk and lifecycle requirements.
Imagine a production API key accidentally appears in a Git commit.
Verify that the new credential works.
Investigate whether the old key was used.
Remove the exposed value from accessible source, logs and other locations.
Review the incident and improve secret-scanning controls.
Do not simply delete the key from the latest source file and assume that the incident is resolved.
Keep actual local secret files out of Git.
Review pull requests for accidental credentials.
The exact ignore patterns should match your project structure. Also remember that .gitignore does not remove files already tracked by Git.
Key takeaway: A secret is a credential, not ordinary application configuration. Protect its complete lifecycle, including creation, access, rotation and revocation.

sections.title: 11. API Logging and Sensitive Data Exposure

blocks.text: Logging is the process of recording important events that occur inside an application.
Logs help developers and security engineers understand:
Which user or service initiated the action.
Whether the action succeeded or failed.
For example, an administrator deletes a course.
A useful security log might record:
Timestamp: 2026-11-27T10:30:00 Event: COURSE_DELETED Actor: admin-101 Resource: course-500 Result: SUCCESS Request ID: req-abc123
This helps investigate activity without exposing sensitive credentials.
11.2 Why are logs important for security?
Imagine someone modifies a student's course progress without permission.
Without appropriate logs, it may be difficult to establish:
Whether the request came from a permitted operation.
Whether similar suspicious requests occurred earlier.
Logging is also important for detecting:
OWASP recommends recording important security events and including logging verification in security testing.
A common backend security mistake is logging complete HTTP requests and responses without considering the information they contain.
Sensitive personal information unless there is a clearly justified and authorized need.
It might expose an Authorization header containing a bearer token.
log.info( "API request: requestId={}, method={}, path={}", requestId, method, sanitizedPath );
OWASP specifically advises removing, masking, hashing or otherwise protecting sensitive values such as passwords, access tokens and session identifiers in logs.
These categories may be implemented through shared logging infrastructure, but they should have clearly defined purposes and access restrictions.
Consider a user changing a course's visibility.
This is an illustrative audit record. The previous and new values should only be included if they are appropriate to retain and do not reveal unnecessary sensitive information.
A well-designed audit system should have:
For high-value operations, consider append-only or tamper-resistant audit storage.
Logs are also an input-handling surface.
Imagine a user submits a course title containing newline characters.
If the application inserts that value into a log message without sanitization, an attacker could manipulate the appearance of log entries.
Use structured logging where possible, validate untrusted values and encode or sanitize characters that could alter the log format.
log.warn( "Invalid course update: actorId={}, courseId={}, result={}", actorId, courseId, "REJECTED" );
Avoid including arbitrary request bodies or unsanitized user-controlled text.
Production backend systems commonly collect application logs in centralized infrastructure.
Search, filter, correlate and investigate events
Detect suspicious activity and application incidents
Key takeaway: Security logging must provide enough evidence to investigate problems without becoming another source of sensitive data exposure.
Security testing is the process of examining an application to identify weaknesses that could be exploited to bypass security controls.
Module 08 taught you how to verify that your backend works correctly.
Module 09 extends that knowledge by asking:
Can someone misuse the application even when its endpoints appear to work correctly?
A course update API may correctly return 200 OK, but if a student can modify a course belonging to another instructor, the API has a security vulnerability.
You must test security requirements separately.
You can use Postman or curl to send requests directly to the backend.
Next, test with separate student accounts and verify that one student cannot access another student's information.
Use only test credentials and synthetic data in your isolated lab.
Helps identify web and API security issues through automated and manual testing.
Useful for authorized security assessments of your own test applications.
Intercepts and inspects HTTP requests and responses, helping security testers investigate API behaviour.
Useful for manually verifying API authentication, request validation, role restrictions and error responses.
Helps detect potentially unsafe code patterns during development.
No single tool can identify every API security vulnerability. In particular, a scanner may not understand your business rules or know which student is permitted to access a particular course.
Manual analysis, automated security tests, code review and threat modeling must work together.
Two important security testing approaches are:

How Module 08 and Module 09 work together
These modules serve different engineering purposes and should be learned together.
For example, Module 08 verifies that a student can retrieve their progress correctly. Module 09 verifies that the same student cannot retrieve someone else's progress.
The central engineering principle of Module 09:

An API is not secure simply because it requires a login, uses HTTPS or hides administrative functionality in the frontend. Every request must be validated, every resource must have appropriate access controls, every sensitive operation must be protected, and every security assumption must be tested.
A professional backend engineer must build APIs that remain secure even when clients send unexpected, manipulated or unauthorized requests.
